introduction-what-actually-runs-my-conta.core: 'Docker' is a stack: the docker CLI talks to dockerd, which delegates to containerd (a high-level runtime managing images, snapshots and container lifecycle), which uses a shim and runc (a low-level OCI runtime) to actually create namespaces and cgroups and start the process. Kubernetes talks to containerd or CRI-O through the CRI, with no Docker daemon needed.

first_principles.problem: Engineers panic when Kubernetes 'removes Docker' without understanding images still work.
derivation: Images are **OCI**, so they run anywhere.

analogy.title: A restaurant order chain
analogy.story: Waiter (CLI), head chef (dockerd), kitchen manager (containerd) and line cook (runc) who actually cooks.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens need every role; Kubernetes skips the 'head chef' (dockerd) entirely.

example.title: Inspecting on a Kubernetes node

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No docker CLI needed on nodes.

code.text:
crictl ps                      # containers via CRI
crictl images
ctr -n k8s.io containers list   # containerd's view

example.outcome: clear picture of what runs containers.

check.q: Which component actually creates the container's namespaces and cgroups?
check.a: The low-level OCI runtime, typically runc.

oci-speaking-the-same-language.core: The Open Container Initiative defines three specs: the image spec (manifests, layers, config), the runtime spec (how to run a filesystem bundle with config.json) and the distribution spec (registry API). Because Docker, Podman, BuildKit, containerd, CRI-O and registries all follow OCI, images built anywhere run anywhere.

first_principles.problem: Teams worry that images built with one tool won't run on another runtime or registry.
derivation: Registries store **other artefacts** too (Helm charts, signatures, SBOMs).

analogy.title: Standard shipping container dimensions
analogy.story: Any ship, crane or truck can handle any container.
analogy.breaks: Physical containers have one format; OCI also stores non-image artefacts like signatures.

check.q: What are the three OCI specifications?

the-standard-layer-cake.core: The runtime layer cake: orchestrator (Kubernetes) → CRI implementation (containerd with its CRI plugin, or CRI-O) → containerd-shim per container (keeps it running if containerd restarts, handles stdio and exit codes) → OCI runtime (runc) that sets up namespaces/cgroups and execs the process, after which runc exits.

first_principles.problem: Restarting containerd on a node is feared to kill all containers.
truths: Shims decouple container lifetime from the daemon.

analogy.title: Lighting a candle with a match
analogy.story: The match (runc) lights it and goes out; the candle holder (shim) keeps it standing.
analogy.breaks: Candles burn out on their own; containers run until stopped or crashed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Containers parented by shims, not containerd.

code.text:
ps -ef --forest | grep -A2 containerd-shim
# containerd-shim-runc-v2 -namespace k8s.io -id abc...
#   \_ nginx: master process

check.q: Why does each container have a containerd-shim?
check.a: So containers keep running and report status independently of the containerd daemon.

the-security-problem-shared-kernels.core: All containers on a host share one kernel. A kernel vulnerability, an over-privileged container (privileged: true, hostPath mounts, CAP_SYS_ADMIN) or a container escape can compromise the whole node and other tenants. Defence involves least privilege (non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only rootfs, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux) and stronger isolation for untrusted code.

first_principles.problem: A container running as root with the Docker socket mounted lets an attacker take over the host.
truths: The kernel is a shared attack surface.

analogy.title: Flats sharing one foundation
analogy.story: Strong doors help, but a crack in the foundation affects every flat.
analogy.breaks: Foundations rarely crack; kernel CVEs appear regularly.

check.q: Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container dangerous?
check.a: It gives the container control over the Docker daemon, effectively root on the host.

sandboxed-runtimes-gvisor-and-firecracke.core: Sandboxed runtimes add a stronger boundary than namespaces. gVisor (runsc) intercepts syscalls with a user-space kernel (Sentry), so containers rarely touch the host kernel directly. Kata Containers and Firecracker run each container or pod inside a lightweight VM with its own kernel. Both trade some performance and compatibility for isolation.

first_principles.problem: A SaaS platform runs customer-supplied code and can't risk a kernel escape.
truths: Fewer host syscalls mean a smaller attack surface.
Hardware virtualisation is a strong boundary.
derivation: **gVisor** for syscall-level sandboxing, low overhead startup.

analogy.title: Interpreters versus separate rooms
analogy.story: gVisor is an interpreter relaying every request; Kata gives each guest their own soundproof room.
analogy.breaks: Interpreters are slow for long talks; gVisor overhead grows with syscall-heavy workloads.

example.title: Choosing isolation
flow: Multi-tenant untrusted with custom kernels → Kata

points: Pay overhead only for risky code.

check.a: It implements the Linux syscall interface in a user-space kernel, so the container's syscalls rarely reach the host kernel.

runtimeclass-selecting-a-runtime-in-kube.core: RuntimeClass is a cluster object naming a runtime handler configured in the node's CRI (e.g. runsc for gVisor, kata for Kata). Pods select it with runtimeClassName, and scheduling fields ensure they land on nodes that support it, with optional overhead accounting for the sandbox's extra resources.

first_principles.problem: Only some pods need sandboxing, but the whole cluster runs one runtime.
truths: Pods need a way to choose.

analogy.title: Choosing a lane at airport security
analogy.story: Standard lane for most travellers, an enhanced screening lane for flagged bags.
analogy.breaks: Airport lanes exist at every terminal; runtimes must be installed on specific nodes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Untrusted pod runs sandboxed on gVisor nodes.

check.q: What does the 'handler' field in a RuntimeClass refer to?
check.a: The runtime handler name configured in the node's CRI (e.g. runsc).
